Denial check runs before the permission check, overriding a fresh permCache allow entry
Cache-hit-but-denied lookups are counted as cache misses in permissionCacheUsage metric, under-reporting hit rate
Real DB errors from GetUserIdentifiers are silently retried as cache misses in the List path, doubling query load and masking the first error
Denial cache key omits identity type, so user and serviceaccount subjects with the same UID string share userPermDenialCacheKey and cross-contaminate denial decisions
Test suite only exercises allow-side fallback and lacks a complementary deny-from-DB-then-re-check test for the security-relevant inverse ordering
permDenialCache has no invalidation path, so stale denial entries can serve denials after permission changes are granted
Deleted the only test asserting cached permissions and added no test covering the denial-becomes-allow transition or permission mutation after populating permDenialCache
Denial-cache-hit path increments permissionCacheUsage metric with "true", conflating permission cache and denial cache hit rates with no test asserting metric values
getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch from getIdentityPermissions, creating parallel hand-maintained enumerations that can drift silently
List path lacks tests for the error branch and outdated cached permission set in getCachedIdentityPermissions, unlike the Check equivalent

Denial cache key embeds raw folder field, so folder vs no-folder requests produce different keys and the cache silently misses for the common empty-ParentFolder case, with no test covering this duality

NoopCache disables caching for the in-process/embedded client, contradicting the PR's intent to improve authz caching; embedded deployments lose the 30s cache and hit a full Check RPC + DB roundtrip per permission check
New denial cache (permDenialCache) has no invalidation path; stale denial entries keep returning Allowed: false after access is granted until shortCacheTTL expires
userPermDenialCacheKey is a parallel hand-maintained key scheme with no shared source of truth with userPermCacheKey, risking silent cache-invalidation divergence on future key format changes
Deletion of the only test asserting getUserPermissions returns cached entries leaves the function's cache contract untested

Stale denial cache in service.go:116-120 is never invalidated (no Delete/Set(false) on permDenialCache) and is read first with no fallback, so it overrides refreshed permission grants for up to shortCacheTTL
Denial decision at service.go:117-119 returns before GetUserIdentifiers and checkPermission run, so cached denials override wildcard permissions like dashboards:* without identity re-validation

Delimiter-collision in userPermDenialCacheKey at cache.go:30-32 uses plain '_' separators with no escaping of request-supplied name/parent, so e.g. name='a_b', parent='' collides with name='a', parent='b', causing cross-resource denials

Unbounded cache cardinality at service.go:56,84: the denial cache stores one entry per (user, action, name, parent) tuple, so denied-request fan-out (e.g. a bot scanning dashboard UIDs) can bloat the shared local cache within the TTL window

Metrics semantics drift at service.go:123-141: a permission cache hit that evaluates to denied is counted as permissionCacheUsage{cached="false"} (a miss), corrupting cache hit-rate metrics for deny-heavy traffic

getCachedIdentityPermissions at service.go:342-367 swallows GetUserIdentifiers errors as cache misses, causing a duplicate identity lookup via getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions on the hot path with no backoff and no logging of the first error

PR titled 'improve authz caching' silently removes caching from the embedded-server client path by replacing newRBACClient (with 30s LocalCache) with NoopCache, regressing the exact behavior the PR claims to improve, with no config flag, comment, or test indicating the sacrifice was intentional

New denial cache (permDenialCache) short-circuits before any permission lookup and has no invalidation path: denial entries live under distinct keys per resource+folder combination, so permission cache invalidation cannot reach them, delaying permission-grant propagation by up to shortCacheTTL

Denial cache is populated from a check based on a stale permission cache and remains pinned for the full TTL even after fresh permissions are loaded; the fresh DB load does not clear or reconcile the denial entry, letting the weaker cache win due to fixed read order

Deleted contract test 'should return permissions from cache if available' for getUserPermissions was not migrated: replacement tests only cover the user identity type, leaving the anonymous-identity cache-hit path and render-service passthrough untested so regressions would pass CI silently

Double permissionCacheUsage accounting on the stale-cache fall-through path: cache-hit-but-denied is counted as a miss ('false'), silently redefining the metric's semantics and inflating miss counts in existing dashboards/alerts with no rename or documentation

permDenialCache has no invalidation path when permissions are granted or resources moved, causing stale deny entries to block legitimate access until shortCacheTTL expires, because the denial key format is distinct from the userPermCacheKey the invalidation path evicts

The deny fast-path in Check returns Allowed:false for all identity types including TypeRenderService, and the denial cache key is computed from checkReq.UserUID without an identity-type component, so a deny written for one identity type can be served for another if UIDs collide across types

Test comment at service_test.go ~970 contradicts its fixture: comment says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked' but the fixture seeds permCache with a deny, so the test fails for the wrong reason (error-vs-deny) and misleads about what it verifies

The new denial-cache behavior in service.go (DB-derived deny populating permDenialCache and second Check served from denial cache) has zero test coverage; no test calls Check twice on a deny or inspects permDenialCache contents
getCachedIdentityPermissions switch branches for TypeAnonymous, TypeRenderService, and default are never hit by any test, so a refactor inverting the TypeRenderService passthrough would ship green

The new permDenialCache is written but never invalidated — permission changes invalidate userPermCacheKey/basicRoleCacheKey but not the denial key, so denied users can see stale 'denied' results past the invalidation contract for up to shortCacheTTL

In Check (service.go:145-166), getCachedIdentityPermissions conflates cache.ErrNotFound with real errors from GetUserIdentifiers, so transient store errors are silently reclassified as cache misses with no log or error metric, corrupting permissionCacheUsage metrics
The cache-hit-then-deny path in Check double-reads by falling through to a second getIdentityPermissions call

Removing the cache check from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions drops caching for any caller other than Check and List, causing silent per-request DB load if other callers exist or are added later

The test guarding that getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions cache results (service_test.go:342-349) was deleted rather than reasserted for the new structure, removing the tripwire against future callers assuming caching exists

Denial cache consulted before permission cache and never invalidated on permission changes; distinct denial key survives exact-key invalidation of userPermCacheKey, so newly granted access is denied until shortCacheTTL expires
Errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions silently discarded in Check, making DB/store failures indistinguishable from cache misses and doubling DB load via immediate duplicate GetUserIdentifiers call

userPermDenialCacheKey joins components with bare underscore separator without escaping, allowing key collisions between different field value combinations so a denial for one resource can deny another
Cached List path never falls back to DB on stale permCache hit, producing silently truncated Items/Folders lists reported as successful, unlike Check which has a deny-then-refetch guard

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache is written but never invalidated on permission changes, so a granted permission can be denied for up to the full TTL

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new negative-result cache `permDenialCache` that is checked first in `Service.Check` and causes an immediate deny (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). The cache is written whenever the DB-backed check returns `!allowed` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`). There is no invalidation or deletion path shown for this cache on permission/role changes; entries only expire by TTL (`newCacheWrap[bool](..., shortCacheTTL)`). This can incorrectly deny a newly-granted permission until TTL expiry, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial check runs before the permission check, overriding a fresh permCache allow entry

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new logic checks `permDenialCache` first and returns `Allowed: false` immediately on a hit (service.go: `if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). This occurs before consulting `permCache` via `getCachedIdentityPermissions` / `checkPermission`, so any denial entry will override what would otherwise be an allow from `permCache`. The accompanying test `TestService_CacheCheck/"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"` explicitly asserts this precedence, suggesting it’s intentional; the main concern is potential staleness/precedence semantics rather than a clearly verifiable defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cache-hit-but-denied lookups are counted as cache misses in permissionCacheUsage metric, under-reporting hit rate

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a cache hit that results in `allowed == false` from `checkPermission` does not increment `permissionCacheUsage` with `"true"`. Instead, execution falls through and unconditionally increments `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action)` (after the cached-perms block), even though `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeded (i.e., the permission map was retrieved from cache). Only explicit `permDenialCache` hits and cached-perms allow results are counted as cache hits. This under-reports cache-hit rate for cached-but-denied checks (even if the fallback-to-DB behavior is intentional).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Real DB errors from GetUserIdentifiers are silently retried as cache misses in the List path, doubling query load and masking the first error

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.List`, the code treats *any* error from `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` as a cache miss and falls back to `getIdentityPermissions(...)` (see `if err == nil { ... } else { ... permissions, err = s.getIdentityPermissions(...) }`). But `getCachedIdentityPermissions` can return real errors (not just `cache.ErrNotFound`), e.g. for `TypeUser/TypeServiceAccount` it calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` and returns that error directly. This means a real DB/store failure from `GetUserIdentifiers` is ignored and the code retries via `getIdentityPermissions`, which likely calls `GetUserIdentifiers` again, doubling load and potentially masking the original error if the second call succeeds.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache key omits identity type, so user and serviceaccount subjects with the same UID string share userPermDenialCacheKey and cross-contaminate denial decisions

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the denial cache key is computed as `userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` and `userPermDenialCacheKey` only includes `(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)`—it does not incorporate `checkReq.IdentityType`. Since `Check` can be called for different identity types (see `getCachedIdentityPermissions` handling `types.TypeUser` and `types.TypeServiceAccount`), two subjects of different identity types that share the same `UserUID` string in the request would share the same denial cache entry, causing cross-contamination of deny decisions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test suite only exercises allow-side fallback and lacks a complementary deny-from-DB-then-re-check test for the security-relevant inverse ordering

adjudication.rationale: Diff adds new caching/negative-caching logic in Service.Check: it first consults permDenialCache (userPermDenialCacheKey), then tries cached permissions (getCachedIdentityPermissions) and only falls back to DB (getIdentityPermissions); if DB result is denied it sets permDenialCache (s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)). The newly added tests in TestService_CacheCheck only cover DB fallback scenarios where the DB ultimately allows ("Fallback to the database on cache miss" and "...outdated cache" both assert Allowed=true), plus a deny case where permDenialCache is pre-seeded manually ("Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"). There is no test where the DB denies on fallback and a subsequent re-check observes the newly-written permDenialCache (or verifies denial-cache precedence after being populated by the code), so the finding is grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permDenialCache has no invalidation path, so stale denial entries can serve denials after permission changes are granted

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `permDenialCache` and makes it authoritative in `Service.Check`: if `permDenialCache.Get(...)` hits, the request is immediately denied without consulting fresh permissions (`return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil`). Denials are written on any non-allowed result (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`). The diff shows no explicit invalidation mechanism tied to permission changes; however entries are stored via `newCacheWrap[bool](cache, ..., shortCacheTTL)`, implying they at least expire on TTL. So the concern about stale denials is grounded (they can persist until TTL), but it’s more an expected caching/consistency tradeoff than a clear defect proven by the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Deleted the only test asserting cached permissions and added no test covering the denial-becomes-allow transition or permission mutation after populating permDenialCache

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove the cache-hit test in `TestService_getUserPermissions` (the block starting at `name: "should return permissions from cache if available"`), and introduces new denial caching logic in `Service.Check` via `permDenialCache` (checked before `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, and set when `!allowed`). While new tests were added to cover cached-allow (`TestService_CacheCheck`/`TestService_CacheList`) and explicit deny (`Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`), there is indeed no test exercising the edge case where a request is denied (thus `permDenialCache` is populated) and later the underlying permission changes to allow within the denial cache TTL (i.e., denial-to-allow transition / permission mutation).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial-cache-hit path increments permissionCacheUsage metric with "true", conflating permission cache and denial cache hit rates with no test asserting metric values

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the early return on a denial-cache hit (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... }`) increments `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action).Inc()`, which is the same metric used for permission-map cache hits/misses. This conflates denial-cache hit rates with permission-cache hit rates. The newly added tests (TestService_CacheCheck/TestService_CacheList) exercise cache behavior but do not assert any metric label/value changes, so this metric semantics issue is untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch from getIdentityPermissions, creating parallel hand-maintained enumerations that can drift silently

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` in `service.go` with a `switch idType` handling `TypeAnonymous`, `TypeRenderService`, `TypeUser`, `TypeServiceAccount`, and a default error. This mirrors the identity-type branching already present in the existing permission-fetching path (`getIdentityPermissions(...)`), creating two separate places that must be updated when identity types or behavior change. That’s a maintainability/architecture risk (silent drift), but the diff does not show an immediate correctness failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: List path lacks tests for the error branch and outdated cached permission set in getCachedIdentityPermissions, unlike the Check equivalent

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new caching behavior to List(): it first calls getCachedIdentityPermissions and on error falls back to getIdentityPermissions (service.go around List). New tests include TestService_CacheList, but it only covers the cache-hit path. Unlike Check(), which now has explicit tests for cache hit, cache miss fallback, and outdated cache fallback (TestService_CacheCheck subtests), there is no analogous List test covering the fallback branch (cache miss / ErrNotFound) or an “outdated cache” scenario where cached permissions don’t include items that the DB would return.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache key embeds raw folder field, so folder vs no-folder requests produce different keys and the cache silently misses for the common empty-ParentFolder case, with no test covering this duality

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the denial cache key is built from `checkReq.ParentFolder` (`userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.ParentFolder)`). From the diff alone, there’s no evidence of a “folder vs no-folder” duality that would create two different representations of “no folder”: an omitted proto string field and an explicitly empty string both serialize to `""`, yielding the same key. The tests do cover denial-cache behavior (`TestService_CacheCheck` "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"), and the diff doesn’t show any case where an empty/unspecified folder would be expected to match a non-empty folder key (that would be a semantic requirement not established in the diff).

adjudication_records.issue_text: NoopCache disables caching for the in-process/embedded client, contradicting the PR's intent to improve authz caching; embedded deployments lose the 30s cache and hit a full Check RPC + DB roundtrip per permission check

adjudication.rationale: In `ProvideAuthZClient`, the embedded/in-process client is changed from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` (which previously wrapped `authzlib.NewClient` with a 30s `cache.NewLocalCache(...)` as seen in the removed `newRBACClient` code) to `authzlib.NewClient(..., authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, which disables the client-side cache for embedded deployments. Remote clients still use a 30s local cache in `newRemoteRBACClient`. This is a concrete diff-grounded performance/behavior change (more Check/List RPCs in embedded mode) rather than a correctness defect; the claim about a DB roundtrip per check is not fully verifiable because the server now has its own caches (`permCache`, `permDenialCache`) that can avoid DB hits even if the client cache is disabled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New denial cache (permDenialCache) has no invalidation path; stale denial entries keep returning Allowed: false after access is granted until shortCacheTTL expires

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is checked first and causes an immediate `Allowed: false` return when the key exists (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). The cache is populated whenever the computed result is denied (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }`). There is no corresponding deletion/override path when permissions later become allowed, and the early-return prevents falling back to DB to observe newly granted access until `shortCacheTTL` expires. This creates stale-deny behavior grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: userPermDenialCacheKey is a parallel hand-maintained key scheme with no shared source of truth with userPermCacheKey, risking silent cache-invalidation divergence on future key format changes

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new cache-key function `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` in `pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go` that independently constructs keys (`namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`) alongside the existing `userPermCacheKey(...)` (`namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action`). These are parallel, hand-maintained string formats with no shared builder/constant/source of truth. While this is not a concrete defect in the current diff, it does create a maintainability risk: future changes to the base permission key format could silently fail to update the denial-key format, leading to inconsistent cache behavior/invalidation assumptions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Deletion of the only test asserting getUserPermissions returns cached entries leaves the function's cache contract untested

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the cache hit path from `getUserPermissions` (and `getAnonymousPermissions`) entirely: the `permCache.Get(...)` logic and related metrics were deleted in `getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions`. Caching is now handled via the newly added `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, which is exercised through new tests `TestService_CacheCheck` and `TestService_CacheList` that assert behavior when permissions are present/missing in cache. Therefore, deleting the old test does not leave a still-existing “getUserPermissions returns cached entries” contract untested—the function no longer has that contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Stale denial cache in service.go:116-120 is never invalidated (no Delete/Set(false) on permDenialCache) and is read first with no fallback, so it overrides refreshed permission grants for up to shortCacheTTL

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new permDenialCache is consulted first (permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(...); if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }) and this path has no fallback to cached perms or the DB. The cache is only ever written on a deny (if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }) and there is no corresponding Delete or overwrite on a later allow in the shown diff. This means a previously cached deny will continue to force-deny until expiry (shortCacheTTL), even if permissions have since changed to allow (which would otherwise be detected by the DB fallback logic added for permCache misses/outdated entries).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial decision at service.go:117-119 returns before GetUserIdentifiers and checkPermission run, so cached denials override wildcard permissions like dashboards:* without identity re-validation

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check(), the new early block checks permDenialCache and immediately returns Allowed:false if the key exists (service.go around the added permDenialKey logic) before calling getCachedIdentityPermissions()/getIdentityPermissions or checkPermission. Since permDenialCache entries are written whenever a prior evaluation returned !allowed, a stale denial can override later-granted permissions (including broader/wildcard permissions) until the short TTL expires, because the rest of the permission evaluation is skipped.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Delimiter-collision in userPermDenialCacheKey at cache.go:30-32 uses plain '_' separators with no escaping of request-supplied name/parent, so e.g. name='a_b', parent='' collides with name='a', parent='b', causing cross-resource denials
matched_golden_ids: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same core problem: cache key creation in userPermDenialCacheKey uses '_' as a delimiter without escaping, allowing ambiguous concatenations when components contain underscores or are empty, leading to key collisions and incorrect denial cache hits affecting permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unbounded cache cardinality at service.go:56,84: the denial cache stores one entry per (user, action, name, parent) tuple, so denied-request fan-out (e.g. a bot scanning dashboard UIDs) can bloat the shared local cache within the TTL window

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `permDenialCache` (`Service` struct) keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` and populates it on every denied check (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`). Since `name` and `parent` are request-controlled and can vary arbitrarily, a client/bot issuing many denied requests with unique `(name,parent)` values will create many distinct cache entries within `shortCacheTTL`. The cache instance is shared with other caches (`newCacheWrap(..., cache, ...)`) and no bound/limit is shown in this diff, so this introduces a realistic memory/resource-exhaustion risk (unbounded cardinality) grounded in the added code path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Metrics semantics drift at service.go:123-141: a permission cache hit that evaluates to denied is counted as permissionCacheUsage{cached="false"} (a miss), corrupting cache hit-rate metrics for deny-heavy traffic

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a cached permissions map can be successfully retrieved (`getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns `err == nil`) but if `checkPermission` evaluates `allowed == false`, the code falls through and increments `permissionCacheUsage` with `cached="false"` (right before calling `getIdentityPermissions`). This makes the metric represent “request answered by cache (allowed)” rather than “cache hit”, which is a semantics drift from prior behavior (previously cache-hit was counted in `getUserPermissions` regardless of allow/deny outcome). It’s observability/metrics correctness/clarity, not a functional defect in authorization behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getCachedIdentityPermissions at service.go:342-367 swallows GetUserIdentifiers errors as cache misses, causing a duplicate identity lookup via getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions on the hot path with no backoff and no logging of the first error

adjudication.rationale: In `Check` and `List`, the result of `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` is treated as a cache-hit only when `err == nil`; any error (including a real `GetUserIdentifiers` failure returned from `getCachedIdentityPermissions`) is effectively treated like a cache miss and the code falls through to `getIdentityPermissions(...)` without logging the first error (see `Check`: new block starting around `permDenialKey := ...` then `cachedPerms, err := ...; if err == nil { ... }` and afterwards always calling `getIdentityPermissions`; similarly in `List`). This can cause duplicated identifier lookups on the hot path (since `getCachedIdentityPermissions` calls `GetUserIdentifiers`, and `getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions` will likely do so again) and hides the initial failure, but it’s more a performance/observability/error-handling concern than a clear correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: PR titled 'improve authz caching' silently removes caching from the embedded-server client path by replacing newRBACClient (with 30s LocalCache) with NoopCache, regressing the exact behavior the PR claims to improve, with no config flag, comment, or test indicating the sacrifice was intentional

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the in-process/embedded client path in `ProvideAuthZClient` was changed from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` (which previously constructed an `authzlib.NewClient` with a 30s `cache.NewLocalCache(...)`) to `authzlib.NewClient(..., authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`. The newly added `NoopCache` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound` on `Get`, effectively disabling client-side caching only for the embedded-server path, while the remote path (`newRemoteRBACClient`) still uses the LocalCache. This is a meaningful behavior/performance change that is not documented or guarded by a flag in the diff, but it does not appear to be a correctness-breaking defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New denial cache (permDenialCache) short-circuits before any permission lookup and has no invalidation path: denial entries live under distinct keys per resource+folder combination, so permission cache invalidation cannot reach them, delaying permission-grant propagation by up to shortCacheTTL

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new permDenialCache is consulted first and immediately returns Allowed:false on a cache hit (permDenialCache.Get(...) then return &CheckResponse{Allowed:false} before any getCachedIdentityPermissions/getIdentityPermissions DB lookup). The denial entry is written whenever a check is denied (permDenialCache.Set(...) when !allowed), and the diff shows no invalidation/deletion mechanism for these denial keys. Because the denial cache key includes namespace+userUID+action+name+parentFolder (userPermDenialCacheKey), it is independent of the existing permCache userPermCacheKey/anonymousPermCacheKey entries and will continue to block access for up to shortCacheTTL even if the underlying permissions are later granted, with no fallback-to-DB path while the denial entry exists.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache is populated from a check based on a stale permission cache and remains pinned for the full TTL even after fresh permissions are loaded; the fresh DB load does not clear or reconcile the denial entry, letting the weaker cache win due to fixed read order

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, an existing denial entry in `permDenialCache` is consulted first and immediately returns `Allowed: false` (lines adding `permDenialKey` check). Denials are then populated on any DB-backed check that results in `!allowed` via `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`, but there is no code path that clears/reconciles that denial entry when a later request is allowed (whether via cached perms returning true or a fresh `getIdentityPermissions` DB load returning true). This means a previously cached denial can continue to override newly-granted permissions until TTL expires. The finding’s “populated from a stale permission cache” part is not shown (denial cache is only set after the DB check), but the pinned-denial/override behavior is verifiable in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Deleted contract test 'should return permissions from cache if available' for getUserPermissions was not migrated: replacement tests only cover the user identity type, leaving the anonymous-identity cache-hit path and render-service passthrough untested so regressions would pass CI silently

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the cache-hit test in `TestService_getUserPermissions` and moves cache-hit behavior into the new `getCachedIdentityPermissions` (used by `Check` and `List`). That new function has distinct branches for `types.TypeAnonymous` (checks `s.permCache` via `anonymousPermCacheKey`) and `types.TypeRenderService` (always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`), but the newly added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only exercise the `types.TypeUser` path (`Subject: "user:test-uid"`). There is no test covering the anonymous cache-hit branch or the render-service passthrough behavior, so regressions in those branches would not be caught by these new tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Double permissionCacheUsage accounting on the stale-cache fall-through path: cache-hit-but-denied is counted as a miss ('false'), silently redefining the metric's semantics and inflating miss counts in existing dashboards/alerts with no rename or documentation

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, if `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns cached perms (cache hit) but `checkPermission` yields `allowed == false`, the code falls through and unconditionally increments `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action)` before querying the DB (`getIdentityPermissions`). This means a cache hit that cannot positively authorize is recorded as a "miss" in the metric, changing/inflating miss semantics for existing dashboards. However, the finding’s "double accounting" wording is not strictly accurate here: the cache-hit-but-denied path does not also increment the "true" label; it only increments the "false" label once.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permDenialCache has no invalidation path when permissions are granted or resources moved, causing stale deny entries to block legitimate access until shortCacheTTL expires, because the denial key format is distinct from the userPermCacheKey the invalidation path evicts

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `permDenialCache` checked first in `Service.Check` (early-return deny on cache hit) and populated on DB-evaluated denies (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`). Within this diff there is no corresponding invalidation/clearing of `permDenialCache` when permissions change, so a previously-denied `(namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder)` tuple can continue to be denied until `shortCacheTTL` expires. However, the finding’s claim about an existing “invalidation path” that evicts `userPermCacheKey` but not `permDenialCache` is not verifiable from the provided diff (no eviction code is shown), so this is best treated as a diff-grounded design/edge-case concern rather than a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The deny fast-path in Check returns Allowed:false for all identity types including TypeRenderService, and the denial cache key is computed from checkReq.UserUID without an identity-type component, so a deny written for one identity type can be served for another if UIDs collide across types

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new deny fast-path computes `permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` and immediately returns `Allowed: false` if that key is present, without incorporating `checkReq.IdentityType` into the key or otherwise scoping it (and without resolving to canonical UID via `GetUserIdentifiers`). The same key is written for any request that evaluates to `!allowed` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`). Therefore, a denial cached for one identity type can be applied to another if `checkReq.UserUID` strings collide across identity types, and it will also deny TypeRenderService requests the same way since the fast-path runs before any identity-type-specific handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test comment at service_test.go ~970 contradicts its fixture: comment says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked' but the fixture seeds permCache with a deny, so the test fails for the wrong reason (error-vs-deny) and misleads about what it verifies
matched_golden_ids: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point out the same contradiction: the test comment claims cached permissions allow access, but the fixture/permCache is seeded with a false/deny for the dashboard scope, so checkPermission will still treat it as not allowed and the test intent is misleading.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The new denial-cache behavior in service.go (DB-derived deny populating permDenialCache and second Check served from denial cache) has zero test coverage; no test calls Check twice on a deny or inspects permDenialCache contents

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new behavior in Service.Check: if a DB-derived decision is deny, it stores `true` in `permDenialCache` (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`) and on subsequent calls it short-circuits to deny if the key is present (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). The added tests cover (a) allow via cached perms, (b) fallback to DB on cache miss/outdated cache, and (c) denying when an explicit denial entry is pre-seeded in `permDenialCache`. However, there is no test that exercises the new “DB deny populates permDenialCache” path and then verifies a second `Check` is served from that denial cache (no test calls `Check` twice on a deny or asserts the cache was populated).

adjudication_records.issue_text: getCachedIdentityPermissions switch branches for TypeAnonymous, TypeRenderService, and default are never hit by any test, so a refactor inverting the TypeRenderService passthrough would ship green

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new logic in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` with distinct behavior for `types.TypeAnonymous` (checks `anonymousPermCacheKey`), `types.TypeRenderService` (always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`), and `default` (returns an error). The newly added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only exercise the user path via `Subject: "user:test-uid"` and do not cover the anonymous/render-service/default branches. That leaves the new branch behavior (especially the `TypeRenderService` forced cache-miss semantics) untested in this PR, so a behavior-changing refactor there could plausibly pass the tests added here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The new permDenialCache is written but never invalidated — permission changes invalidate userPermCacheKey/basicRoleCacheKey but not the denial key, so denied users can see stale 'denied' results past the invalidation contract for up to shortCacheTTL

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `permDenialCache` and uses it to short-circuit `Check` to `Allowed: false` when a denial key exists (`Service.Check`: `permDenialCache.Get` early-return; and `permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` on a computed denial). Within this diff, there is no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation path for these denial entries—only TTL-based expiry via `newCacheWrap[bool](..., shortCacheTTL)`. The finding’s broader claim about existing invalidation for `userPermCacheKey`/`basicRoleCacheKey` is not verifiable from the shown diff, but the specific concern that denial entries can remain stale until `shortCacheTTL` is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In Check (service.go:145-166), getCachedIdentityPermissions conflates cache.ErrNotFound with real errors from GetUserIdentifiers, so transient store errors are silently reclassified as cache misses with no log or error metric, corrupting permissionCacheUsage metrics

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the code treats any non-nil error from getCachedIdentityPermissions the same as a cache miss: it only branches on `if err == nil { ... }` and otherwise falls through, increments `permissionCacheUsage` as "false", and proceeds to `getIdentityPermissions` without logging the original error. Since getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors from `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` (not just `cache.ErrNotFound`), those errors can be silently ignored (and mis-attributed as cache misses) if the subsequent DB path succeeds. This is an observability/metrics accuracy issue grounded in the diff, not a clearly broken correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The cache-hit-then-deny path in Check double-reads by falling through to a second getIdentityPermissions call

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, even if `getCachedIdentityPermissions` hits `permCache` successfully, the code only returns early when `allowed` is true. If the cached permissions evaluate to `allowed == false`, it falls through and calls `getIdentityPermissions` (DB-backed) anyway. This matches the finding’s “cache-hit-then-deny falls through to a second getIdentityPermissions call” behavior. However, the diff also adds `permDenialCache` and a comment/test suggesting this is intentional to avoid false negatives from stale/partial cached permission maps; it’s more of a performance/behavior tradeoff than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Removing the cache check from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions drops caching for any caller other than Check and List, causing silent per-request DB load if other callers exist or are added later

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the `permCache.Get(...)` fast-paths inside `getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions` (see deletions around `userPermKey := ...` and `anonPermKey := ...`). Caching is now only consulted via the new `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)`, which is called explicitly from `Service.Check` and `Service.List`. If any other (current or future) call path invokes `getIdentityPermissions`/`getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` without first calling `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, it will no longer read from cache and will hit the store/DB every time. The diff doesn’t prove other callers exist today, but it does create this scope/architecture footgun where cache-read is no longer co-located with permission fetch methods.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The test guarding that getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions cache results (service_test.go:342-349) was deleted rather than reasserted for the new structure, removing the tripwire against future callers assuming caching exists

adjudication.rationale: The deleted test covered a behavior that no longer exists: `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` no longer read from `s.permCache` (the cache-hit branches were removed in `service.go` around `getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions`). Cache reads were refactored into the new `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and are now exercised via new tests `TestService_CacheCheck` and `TestService_CacheList`, which validate cache-hit and fallback behavior at the `Check`/`List` entrypoints. So the test was not deleted “rather than reasserted”; it was replaced with tests aligned to the new caching structure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache consulted before permission cache and never invalidated on permission changes; distinct denial key survives exact-key invalidation of userPermCacheKey, so newly granted access is denied until shortCacheTTL expires

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new permDenialCache is consulted first and causes an immediate deny (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). When permissions are later fetched from DB and `allowed` becomes true, there is no code to clear or invalidate the existing denial entry; the only write is `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`. This makes a prior cached denial for the (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) key override newly granted access until the denial TTL expires.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions silently discarded in Check, making DB/store failures indistinguishable from cache misses and doubling DB load via immediate duplicate GetUserIdentifiers call

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the result of `getCachedIdentityPermissions` is only used when `err == nil`; any non-nil error (including errors from `GetUserIdentifiers` inside `getCachedIdentityPermissions`) is treated the same as a cache miss and not logged, then the code immediately falls back to `getIdentityPermissions` (`permissions, err := s.getIdentityPermissions(...)`). For user/service-account identities, that fallback will call `GetUserIdentifiers` again via `getUserPermissions` (it still computes `userPermKey` from `userIdentifiers`), creating a duplicated lookup in the error path and making cache-miss metrics/behavior indistinguishable from cache/identifier lookup errors. This is a real performance/observability issue shown by the diff, but not a clear functional correctness defect (the DB error would still surface if it persists).

adjudication_records.issue_text: userPermDenialCacheKey joins components with bare underscore separator without escaping, allowing key collisions between different field value combinations so a denial for one resource can deny another

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` which builds the cache key by simple string concatenation with `_` separators: `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Since there is no escaping or length-prefixing, different tuples of `(action, name, parent)` can produce identical keys when any component contains `_` (e.g., `action="a_b", name="c"` vs `action="a", name="b_c"`), and `Service.Check` treats a cache hit as an unconditional deny (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). This creates a real possibility of incorrect denials due to key collisions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cached List path never falls back to DB on stale permCache hit, producing silently truncated Items/Folders lists reported as successful, unlike Check which has a deny-then-refetch guard

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.List`, the code now explicitly prefers `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` and, on cache hit (`err == nil`), proceeds to `listPermission(...)` without any possibility of detecting staleness or refetching from DB (unlike `Service.Check`, which only returns early on cached *allow* and otherwise falls back to `getIdentityPermissions`). If `permCache` is stale/incomplete, `List` can return a truncated `Items`/`Folders` set while still succeeding. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral concern, but whether it is a “defect” depends on intended cache semantics for List; the diff alone doesn’t establish that List must be strongly consistent.
